title: Chapter 1 — Exchanging While Not-Knowing
paragraphs: Chapter 1 asks how Samoan migrants live inside two exchange systems that run on opposite principles: capitalist exchange, felt to be acultural, and Samoan ritual exchange — fa’alavelave — felt to be cultural. Weddings, funerals, and title bestowals pull cash and goods out of the capitalist world and into the ritual one. Gershon's key claim is that Samoans keep the two apart not through the objects they use (a soda can can stand in for a coconut without controversy) but through how knowledge circulates — and especially through deliberate not-knowing.

This strategic ignorance is the chapter's signature idea. No one knows exactly how much money anyone else really has, and both sides keep it that way. The elicitor — usually a senior relative asking for contributions — ignores the capitalist limits on the person being asked, treating relatives as nearly boundless resources. The elicitee — usually a younger relative — hides money in several accounts or with friends so they can plausibly say they cannot give, preserving room to pay the rent. This mutual not-knowing is a productive strategy, and people said it became more useful, not less, after migration.

Gershon sets this against the classic anthropology of "spheres of exchange" (Bohannan), which explained boundaries between economic worlds by the objects allowed to move through them. She flips the question: the spheres are not given by objects; they must be actively produced through the circulation of knowledge. Samoans, she notes, are not anxious about "purifying" modern commodities to make them fit for ritual — commodity fetishism is not what troubles them.

Strikingly, she found almost no critiques of capitalism in her notes. Instead people idealized it, faulting other Samoans as "bad capitalists" or lamenting their own failure to save. Her reading: family demands force her interlocutors to treat money as a commodity with immediate use rather than as capital that could grow — so they are, in effect, "bad Samoan capitalists." One woman noted the money she had sent home over the years could have bought a house.

Using Bradd Shore, Gershon lays out the mechanics. Fa’alavelave publicly display a family's strength and forge its unity while marking its boundaries. Shore's two types matter for the exam: indirect exchange, where every family gives to the same recipient (a church) and competes to look most generous as donations are read aloud; and complementary (direct) exchange, where the two sides give fundamentally unlike things — the bride's side gives fine mats (‘ie toga), which carry only exchange-value, and the groom's side gives use-value goods like food, cloth, and increasingly cash.

Behind the calm public display lies frantic private elicitation, secret record-keeping, and last-minute scrambling; the performance of unity hides the discord of pooling resources. A child's T-shirt captures the double-bind — "I love my aiga, but I hate fa’alavelave." The harshest condemnation is reserved for those who improperly merge the two systems: orators who crash unrelated funerals to collect gifts, or ministers rumoured to pocket offerings. Nostalgia for Samoa, Gershon suggests, is really nostalgia for a time when resources were visibly finite and one did not have to juggle two systems at once.
